about_carthage_body: Punic stelae, Roman Africa proconsularis, and the Byrsa hill remain the oldest onomastic layer of Tunisian genealogy — names, places, and Mediterranean crossings that still echo in family memory.
about_civil_body: État civil from 1886 onward, Protectorate cadastre, and republican identity papers connect living families to the older documentary chain — 24 governorates, one indexed research surface.
about_cta_title: Begin with a name, a governorate, or a register
about_etat_civil_body: Birth, marriage, and death registers from 1886, indexed by governorate.
about_habous_body: Pious endowments tying families to olive groves, fondouks, and medina houses.
about_hero_subtitle: From Punic Carthage and Fatimid Kairouan to Ottoman sijillat and modern état civil, Roots Tunisia holds family evidence across twenty-four governorates.
about_hero_title: A Tunisian archive of names, places, and periods
about_kairouan_body: The Aghlabid and Fatimid capital preserved nasab chains, waqf deeds, and jurisprudential manuscripts. Kairouan remains a primary key for tracing scholarly and tribal lineages across the Sahel and the interior.
about_kairouan_panel_intro: Kairouan’s manuscript culture and pious endowments are not decoration. They are how families recorded descent, property, and scholarship from the Aghlabids through the Hafsids.
about_kairouan_panel_title: Nasab, waqf, and the Great Mosque
about_map_intro: Click a region to read its archival holdings and notable lineages — from Carthage and the Cap Bon to Djerba, the Djérid, and the northwest.
about_method_step_1_desc: We cross-examine ancestral nicknames, kunyas, and governorate origins against geographical registries and tribal confederation rolls.
about_method_step_2_desc: Court deeds, marriage contracts, and habous endowments establish unassailable legal parentage across centuries.
about_method_step_3_desc: Connecting 1886-present records with pre-colonial ancestry to render interactive D3 genealogical visualizations.
about_methodology_title: From oral lineage to verified documentary trees
about_mission_intro: Tunisian families are documented in more than one script, court, and language. A pedigree may begin with a CIN extract in Sousse, pass through a Tunis qadi sijill, and rest on a habous deed in Kairouan. Roots Tunisia keeps those layers together.
about_mission_title: Why Tunisian genealogy needs its own house
about_seo_desc: Roots Tunisia preserves Tunisian lineage through Carthage, Kairouan, Ottoman sijillat, civil registry, and the 24 governorates.
about_seo_title: About Roots Tunisia — Carthage to the civil registry
about_sijillat_body: Charaïque court registers, beylical decrees, and majba tax rolls document marriages, inheritances, and habous from Tunis, Sfax, and the medinas. These sijillat are the backbone of pre-colonial pedigree work.
about_sijillat_panel_intro: Sijillat from charaïque courts, beylical chancery, and majba rolls name spouses, witnesses, neighbourhoods, and estates. They sit beside Protectorate état civil rather than beneath it.

dossier_summary_all_tunisia: Tunisia's genealogical heritage spans 24 governorates uniting Mediterranean coastal ports, Andalusian-settled valleys, Roman-Berber high plains, and Saharan oases.
dossier_summary_central_west: Anchored by Kairouan — fourth holiest city of Islam and capital of medieval Ifriqiya — alongside the Byzantine-Roman high steppes of Sbeitla (Kasserine) and Sidi Bouzid.
dossier_summary_greater_tunis: Encompassing Tunis, Ariana, Ben Arous, and Manouba, Greater Tunis has served as the political, scholarly, and commercial heart of Tunisia since the Hafsid Sultanate.
dossier_summary_north: Strategic Mediterranean port region anchored by Bizerte, ancient Utica, and the Andalusian-Ottoman naval harbor of Ghar El Melh (Porto Farina).
dossier_summary_north_east: Fertile peninsula of Nabeul, Hammamet, Kelibia, and Soliman paired with the mountain springs of Zaghouan — Tunisia's premier heartland of Andalusian Morisco heritage.
dossier_summary_north_west: Uniting Béja, Jendouba, El Kef, and Siliana across the fertile Medjerda valley, Khroumirie forests, and historic fortress cities of the Tell.
dossier_summary_sahel: Historic coastal belt of olive groves, Aghlabid ribats, Fatimid capitals, and ancient merchant towns stretching from Sousse and Monastir to Mahdia and El Jem.
dossier_summary_south_east: From the walled merchant medina of Sfax and the coastal oasis of Gabès to the island of Djerba and the fortified Amazigh hilltop ksour of Medenine and Tataouine.
dossier_summary_south_west: Spanning Gafsa, Tozeur, and Kebili around Chott el-Djerid — a storied region of prehistoric Capsian sites, palm oases, scholar-poets, and trans-Saharan caravan routes.

gov_desc_jendouba: Home to the subterranean Roman villas of Bulla Regia, ancient Numidian Chemtou, Tabarka coral coast, and Ain Draham oak forests.
gov_desc_kairouan: Spiritual and scholarly capital of the Maghreb founded in 670 CE by Uqba ibn Nafi; seat of the Aghlabid dynasty and Maliki jurists.
gov_desc_kasserine: High steppe crossroads beneath Mount Chaambi (Tunisia's highest peak), encompassing Roman-Byzantine Sufetula (Sbeitla) and Cillium.
gov_desc_kebili: Heart of the Nefzaoua oases between Chott el-Djerid and the Grand Erg Oriental dunes, anchored by Kebili and Douz, Gateway to the Sahara.
gov_desc_le_kef: Highland citadel city (Sicca Veneria) near Table de Jugurtha, historic cultural crossroads of Sufi orders, music, and scholarship.
gov_desc_mahdia: 10th-century Fatimid Caliphate capital on a fortified peninsula, renowned for silk weaving, Skifa Kahla, and the El Jem Amphitheatre.
gov_desc_manouba: Fertile lower Medjerda plains, sanctuary of Lella Manoubia, Andalusian town of Tebourba, and historic Beylical Rose Palace.
gov_desc_medenine: Uniting the UNESCO World Heritage Island of Djerba, the coastal peninsula of Zarzis, and the vaulted ghorfa ksour of Medenine and Beni Khedache.
gov_desc_monastir: Ancient Ruspina, 796 CE coastal Ribat fortress of Harthama ibn A'yan, textile guilds of Ksar Hellal, and birthplace of Habib Bourguiba.
gov_desc_nabeul: The Cap Bon peninsula: ceramic guilds of Nabeul, Andalusian town of Soliman, citrus groves of Beni Khalled, and Kelibia fortress.
gov_desc_sfax: Southern economic capital with an intact 9th-century walled Medina, suburban borj garden estates (jnens), and the Kerkennah Islands.
gov_desc_sidi_bouzid: Central agricultural steppes and pastoral plains around Mount Bouhedma, historic homeland of the Hammama confederation.
gov_desc_siliana: Highlands of the Tunisian Dorsal housing the Numidian-Roman city of Mactaris (Makthar) and the ancient site of Zama Regia.
gov_desc_sousse: The Pearl of the Sahel: Punic-Roman Hadrumetum, 9th-century Aghlabid Ribat and Great Mosque, and thriving coastal merchant city.
gov_desc_tataouine: Southern Dahar plateau famed for its multi-story fortified granaries (Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ksar Ezzahra) and hilltop Amazigh villages of Chenini and Douiret.
gov_desc_tozeur: Capital of Bled el-Djerid, famed for Ouled el-Hadef brick architecture, Ibn Chabbat's hydraulic canals, Nefta's Sufi zawiyas, and Abu al-Qasim al-Shabbi.
gov_desc_tunis: Capital of the Republic, historic seat of the Husainid Beys, ancient Carthage, and spiritual center of Zitouna University.
gov_desc_zaghouan: Mountain spring supplying ancient Carthage with water via the Roman Aqueduct, and historic Morisco haven famous for rosewater.

guide_step1_desc: Present your National Identity Card (CIN) or Passport at the reception desk. A personal researcher card is issued on-site granting reading room access.
guide_step2_desc: Consult the paper inventories or online OPAC to find the archival classification (Série, Carton, Registre). Submit up to 3 call slips per research session.
guide_step3_desc: General administrative records become public after 30 years. Civil registry and judicial inheritance records protect personal privacy for 100 years unless direct ascendance is legally proven.
guide_step4_desc: Non-flash personal photography is permitted for most public series. High-resolution certified reproductions can be ordered at the digital laboratory desk.

period_aghabid_note: Scholarly chains of transmission among Kairouan jurists provide Tunisia’s oldest continuous recorded lineages.
period_aghabid_records: Kairouan biographical dictionaries (tabaqat), nasab lineage chains, early waqf deeds.
period_contemporary_note: Collaborative digital genealogy reconnects diaspora branches across the Mediterranean and beyond.
period_contemporary_records: Digitized civil databases, municipal registries, oral history testimonies, and archival restorations.
period_context_body: Contextualize your ancestors across Aghlabid, Hafsid, Andalusian, Ottoman Beylical, Protectorate, and modern eras.
period_hafsid_note: Tunis emerges as imperial capital; mercantile, scholarly, and Andalusian refugee families appear in continuous records.
period_hafsid_records: Hafsid chancery registers, qadi court rulings, family endowment deeds (habous), and scholar ijazat.
period_independence_note: The Code of Personal Status unifies family law, creating modern verifiable civil lineages across Tunisia.
period_independence_records: National civil registry, CIN identity cards, nationality files, and municipal rolls.
period_ottoman_note: The richest pre-modern documentary layer: inheritance and marriage cases systematically name three to four generations.
period_ottoman_records: Charaïque court sijillat, habous deeds, beylical decrees, majba tax registers, and corporation rolls.
period_protectorate_note: Systematic civil registration begins in 1886; fixed family surnames become formalized across all governorates.
period_protectorate_records: État civil registers, cadastre land titles, caïdat files, Sadiki and school registers, ANOM records.
period_punic_note: No unbroken lineage records survive, but ancestral names and territorial toponyms persist in Tunisian heritage.
period_punic_records: Votive stelae from the Tophet, Punic onomastics, Neo-Punic commemorative inscriptions.
period_roman_note: Latin inscriptions document family groupings, civic magistrates, and freedmen across Tunisian cities.
period_roman_records: Funerary epigraphy, municipal alba, land surveys, El Jem and Dougga inscriptions.
period_vandal_note: Ecclesiastical records predominate; onomastic transitions reflect demographic evolution in urban centres.
period_vandal_records: Ecclesiastical councils, episcopal lists, Christian Latin funerary texts, and fortress foundations.
